title: How do you keep up with testing your builds when developing with AI?
author: Aggressive_Cow6961
selftext:
I’m curious what everyone does to make sure their game is still working properly when using AI heavily in development.

It seems like a lot of ppl still rely on manually playtesting after changes to see if anything broke, and visually checking things like UI, animations, interactions, etc.

Has anyone found a better workflow for keeping up with this as you make changes faster with AI?

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
1. You just gotta do it. Maybe it slows you down, but if you don’t test, maybe half your game is broken before you realize. 

1. Good code is kore robust. Good isolation between different parts of your code, so changing one part of your code affects only one part of your game, most of the time.

replies.author: Aggressive_Cow6961
replies.body:
Yeah, that makes sense. I guess the part I keep wondering about is whether “you just gotta do it” has to mean manually replaying the same scenarios every time.

Good code isolation definitely reduces how much can break, but there’s still that last-mile question of whether the game actually behaves the way you expect after each build. Feels like there should be a better way to continuously check the repetitive stuff without having to play through it all yourself.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: If you’re checking repetitive stuff continuously, I don’t think that’s quite right. Like, if you are making changes to enemy behavior, it shouldn’t affect player movement, or particle effect triggers, or level transitions. At least, most of the time.

replies.author: Aggressive_Cow6961
replies.body: I get it. I guess since I'm vibe coding, I can't be ease in my mind whether anything was touched when I'm changing things.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: I check which files are touched after every change, at the bare minimum, and commit after each task

replies.author: Charming_You_25
replies.body: \+1 for kore robust. After my demo I had fable look up the top 10 books on programming and take the main ideas and write them as invariants. No upward imports for example. I also had it so no files (with a few exceptions, like routes) over 500 lines… it’s made my codebase massive but that plus no upward imports also forced compartmentalization.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: Autocorrect didn’t save me that time!

comments.author: tb5841
comments.body: Decent, comprehensive unit tests should help a lot.

replies.author: Aggressive_Cow6961
replies.body: Have you found a good way to do it?

replies.author: tb5841
replies.body:
I haven't actually introduced any tests yet, but I've been looking into GDUnit and it looks promising (Godot). I plan on adding them soon.

In my day job (web development) we have thousands of tests and they are fantastic at catching regression issues. AI is pretty good at wtiting them as well.

comments.author: Affectionate_Fact854
comments.body:
Test suites lots and lots of test suites 
And yet still occasionally doing manual test runs

replies.author: Aggressive_Cow6961
replies.body: does it mean that you automated testing the test suites

comments.author: GuyFromArtClass
comments.body: Make a sand box level to test interactions and behaviors in controlled environments.

replies.author: Aggressive_Cow6961
replies.body: This is a good point!

comments.author: mindsandmyths
comments.body:
You'll always need some manual testing, but there are a lot of strategies to bring that down.

1. Lots of unit testing, like others have suggested.
2. A headless build the AI can "play" to some extent, including taking screenshots. Lets it check more things are working itself, though how hard this is to do varies with the type of game.
3. Include a step in your AI dev's process where it rolls out a sub agent for a code check. Having an agent not encumbered with the existing dev work look at it can be surprisingly effective at finding issues.
4. Ultimately, you do need to do some manual testing after every large chunk of work. 1-3 just increase the size of that work chunk.

comments.author: Charming_You_25
comments.body:
\#1 Browser tests before calling it done and send me screenshots. LLMs love writing tests, lots of those tests are just for the api and don’t check it actually is wired into gameplay.  
\#2 Before promoting significant changes to prod run a long horizon playtest that each have things they’re trying to achieve.  
\#3 I have an “flag for edit queue” button for dev mode. So I can pick in the browser and write copy or flag it for directions. Edit queue is auto picked up and implemented, tested in browser, and promoted.

replies.author: Aggressive_Cow6961
replies.body:
over 15k sounds amazing........ and overwhelming hahaha  
So did you set up this workflow yourself?

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: Not sure if new AIs already set up standard tests, but I've had instructions for AI to create standard tests with each implementation plan which are run automatically by scripts on new runs. The AI doesn't have to manually create these each time, the script runs, tests specific things, and reports back pass or failure. On failure then the AI has to investigate what broke the thing, or if the test is no longer valid for some reason (or needs to be reworked). This removes so many fail cases it's crazy. It does not mean you don't have to do manual testing, but the larger your game gets, the more necessary this is or else you'll spend 99% of your time debugging random crashes when an AI misinterprets the name of a function and decides it can be used for something it shouldn't be.

replies.author: Aggressive_Cow6961
replies.body: You mean like skills? I guess it would be a big help for sure if AI can automatically check my game builds although it will not completely remove my duty to do manually testing.

replies.author: Charming_You_25
replies.body: Yes. I was experimenting full time with full agent workflows for like a year before starting my game, it was.. painful a year ago. But luckily a week after I started my game fable came out and full auto dev became feasible. My process was based on dumber model limitations, which has come in handy because even though the models have gotten smarter the codebase has grown so much it cannot fit in context. There are other things I started off doing the new models have made inefficient, like orchestration loops. Others I’m glad i set up the project from the start, like a list of invariants. So a model can look at something questionable and check if it violates an existing invariant.

replies.author: Aggressive_Cow6961
replies.body: It was a very clever move that you set your agent workflow before you start building your game!

replies.author: Charming_You_25
replies.body: Thanks, writing was on the wall for my job, I had to figure out wtf I was doing because the future was coming fast. The game came about partly because after figuring out what I was doing I was looking for how to apply my knowledge so I decided to build my [dream game!](https://effectco.game) It should be out soon… my guy just said he found the smoking gun.

comments.author: Aggressive_Cow6961
comments.body: somebody replied about the headless testing but the moment I replied to that comment the original comment got deleted. Does anybody have tried headless testing? Which tool have you used?

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: See my other posts. AIs can set up scripts that can be run without burning a billion credits (outside of them getting pass/failure results) automatically whenever the build changes. You should request it in your MDs or explicitly with each plan.

replies.author: Charming_You_25
replies.body: Playwright cli is the move! Especially for Claude which struggles to know how to browser test and by default wants a real browser. Codex seems to be able to figure it out

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: I let AI run early tests for mechanical/performance issues first which can be identified  from profilers and debuggers. And then I go in manually to do the finetuning of the implementation.

comments.author: Unique-Watercress225
comments.body: is there a tool for something like this?

comments.author: Blake9712
comments.body: I just test it a bunch really. Figure If I don’t enjoy my game who will.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body: AIs can playtest for you if you want; it is very costly but it works... watching AI controlling the character and trying  stuff out to test is a wild experience. you should give it a try...

comments.author: Equal-Border-7793
comments.body: I typically have AI run the tests, then I perform a few manual tests myself after multiple AI runs to review the results.

replies.author: Aggressive_Cow6961
replies.body: What kind of stuff can you offload to AI vs you need to manually check?

replies.author: Equal-Border-7793
replies.body: For instance, during the testing process, I manually perform a test after every few successful runs; I treat this as a milestone success and back up the data. Additionally, I generally conduct a manual review of core, critical functions and the final results.

comments.author: KnownPride
comments.body:
you cannot skip this step. Only by playing the game you can gain real feel how the game is. 

As for heavy testing on bug etc you can just make bots to play your game and brute force test it.  
But first step is important.

comments.author: Such--Balance
comments.body:
I create a lot of test environments inside a seperate space in my game project to rapidly test and itterate attacks, visuals and stuff like that without it effecting my main all that much. All parameters visable on screen with sliders to change them. Implemented in there is a save function to export whichever stats and parameters i land on. This file i use to basically copy said attack/visual or whatever to my main and ai will link it up properly there.


Im a total noob though. Im sure this could be refined to way better and faster test environments.
